content_html:
Brain signals

Signals in the brain are transmitted both electrically and chemically, depending on the stage of communication. The process works in two main phases — electrical conduction within neurons and chemical transmission between neurons.

Stage Type Medium Description
Within neuron Electrical Ion flow (Na⁺, K⁺) Action potential travels along axon
Between neurons Chemical Neurotransmitters Cross synapse to activate next neuron
Hybrid point Electrochemical Calcium-mediated vesicle release Links electrical signal to chemical transmission

Electrical Signalling (Within Neurons)

  • Mechanism: Inside each neuron, information travels as an electrical impulse called an action potential.
  • How it works: A neuron’s membrane maintains a voltage difference (resting potential) of about –70 mV. When stimulated (by sensory input or another neuron), ion channels open and allow sodium (Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺) ions to flow, changing the charge distribution. This shift in charge travels down the axon — a wave of depolarisation and repolarisation — like a spark along a wire.
  • Speed: Depending on myelination (insulating sheath around axons), these impulses can travel at up to 120 metres per second.

Chemical Signalling (Between Neurons)

  • Mechanism: When the electrical impulse reaches the axon terminal, it triggers the release of neurotransmitters — the brain’s chemical messengers.
  • How it works: The electrical signal opens voltage-gated calcium channels. Calcium ions (Ca²⁺) enter, causing vesicles filled with neurotransmitter molecules to fuse with the membrane. Neurotransmitters are released into the synaptic cleft (a gap ~20–40 nanometres wide), they bind to receptors on the next neuron’s dendrite, generating a new electrical response.
  • Examples of neurotransmitters:
    • Glutamate — main excitatory signal
    • GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid) — main inhibitory signal
    • Dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine, norepinephrine — modulate mood, attention, and movement.

Integration

This electrochemical signalling allows the brain to:

  • Process information rapidly (via electrical spikes)
  • Modulate responses flexibly (via diverse neurotransmitters)
  • Store and adapt connections over time (through synaptic plasticity)

Electrical signals transmit information within neurons, while chemical signals transmit information between neurons; the brain’s communication network is therefore electrochemical — both fast and adaptive.

Body signals

Signal transmission in the brain and in the body both rely on electrical and chemical mechanisms, but they differ in scale, medium, and speed depending on the target and the pathway.

Within the Brain: Local, Dense, and Chemical–Electrical

Feature Description
Medium Neurons communicating via synapses — extremely short distances (nanometres).
Signal Type Electrochemical: electrical impulses (action potentials) within neurons → neurotransmitter release across synapses.
Speed Very fast (up to 120 m/s) due to short distances and myelinated axons.
Precision Highly specific — single neurons can target exact dendritic spines; networks are densely interconnected.
Neurotransmitters Many types (glutamate, GABA, dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine, etc.) — each with different effects on cognition, emotion, and movement.
Purpose Rapid information processing, perception, memory, decision-making, and coordination of all body functions.

The brain’s communication network is like a city-wide data network — billions of nodes (neurons) connected by ultra-short links, constantly updating in real time.

In the Body: Long-Distance and Mixed Signalling

The body uses two main systems for transmitting signals beyond the brain:

a. Nervous System (Electrical & Chemical)

Feature Description
Medium Peripheral nerves extending from the spinal cord to muscles, glands, and sensory organs.
Signal Type Electrical along axons → chemical at neuromuscular junctions or organ synapses.
Example Motor neuron sends an action potential → releases acetylcholine at the muscle → muscle contracts.
Speed Very fast (milliseconds).
Purpose Immediate control — reflexes, movement, sensation, balance.

Analogy: Like high-speed cables connecting the brain to distant devices (muscles and organs).

b. Endocrine System (Chemical Only)

Feature Description
Medium Hormones released into the bloodstream.
Signal Type Chemical only — hormones travel via circulation.
Example The hypothalamus in the brain triggers the pituitary → releases hormones like ACTH → stimulates adrenal glands to produce cortisol.
Speed Slow (seconds to hours).
Purpose Long-term regulation — growth, metabolism, stress response, reproduction.

Analogy: Like sending a message through the postal system — slower but widespread and sustained.

Feature Comparison

Feature Brain Body (Nervous System) Body (Endocrine System)
Type of Signal Electrical & Chemical Electrical & Chemical Chemical only
Transmission Medium Synapses between neurons Nerves to muscles/organs Bloodstream
Distance Micrometres Centimetres to metres Entire body
Speed Milliseconds Milliseconds Seconds to hours
Precision Extremely high Targeted but broader Low (systemic)
Function Cognition, coordination Movement, reflexes Regulation, growth, stress
Example Molecules Glutamate, GABA Acetylcholine, norepinephrine Insulin, cortisol, adrenaline

The Brain–Body Dialogue

The brain continuously exchanges information with the body through neural and hormonal loops:

  • The hypothalamus acts as a bridge — controlling both nerves and hormones.
  • Signals from the vagus nerve inform the brain about heart rate, gut state, and inflammation.
  • The autonomic nervous system (sympathetic & parasympathetic) fine-tunes heart rate, digestion, and respiration.

Three signalling regimes: brain (fast, local synapses), peripheral nerves (fast, long-range to specific effectors), and endocrine hormones (slow, systemic).

In essence, the brain handles fast, local computation and control, the body uses nerves for rapid action and hormones for long-term coordination. Together, they form a hierarchical and adaptive electrochemical communication system.
